A flexible piece of material — cloth, rope, leather, or strap — that wraps around or cradles something to either support it or send it flying.

That image is the soul of the word "sling." Every meaning below grows from it.

1. A Support for an Injured Arm (Medical Sling)

This is the most common meaning in everyday life. A medical sling is a triangular piece of cloth tied around your neck that acts like a small hammock for your arm. If you break your wrist or injure your shoulder, a doctor places your arm inside this cloth and loops it behind your neck. Your arm rests in it, raised and still, while it heals. The cloth takes the weight off so you don't have to.

"He walked into class with his arm in a sling, still sore from the cricket accident."

2. A Carrier for a Baby (Baby Sling)

A baby sling is a long, wide strip of fabric that a parent ties or wraps over one or both shoulders, creating a snug pocket against their chest or hip. The baby sits or lies in this pocket, held close to the parent's body. The great advantage is that the parent's hands remain completely free.

"She wore her sleeping infant in a sling while she cooked."

3. An Ancient Weapon for Hurling Stones

Long before guns, bows, or cannons, humans used slings as weapons. A sling in this sense was a simple handheld tool: a small leather or cloth pouch with two long cords attached to its ends. The user placed a smooth stone inside the pouch, gripped both cords, and swung the whole thing rapidly in a circle above their head. At just the right moment, they released one cord — and the stone shot out at high speed toward the target.

Skilled slingers could hurl a stone with tremendous force and surprising accuracy. Soldiers, shepherds, and hunters all used them. The most famous example in history is the biblical story of David, a young shepherd who killed the towering warrior Goliath with a single stone launched from his sling.

"David picked up five smooth stones from the stream and loaded one into his sling."

4. A Carrying Strap for Rifles or Bags (Carrying Sling)

A sling can also be a long strap — usually made of leather, nylon, or fabric — attached to an object so it can be hung over the shoulder or worn across the body. The most common example is a gun sling: a strap threaded through two rings on a rifle that lets a soldier or hunter carry the weapon on their back without using their hands.

Bag slings (sometimes called sling bags) work the same way — a single strap worn diagonally across the chest, with the bag hanging at your side or back.

"The hunter slung the rifle over his shoulder using the leather sling."

5. A Loop Used to Lift Heavy Objects (Industrial Sling)

In construction, shipping, and industry, a sling is a heavy-duty loop of rope, chain, wire, or thick nylon used to cradle and lift large, heavy objects with a crane. Workers wrap the sling around or under the object — a steel beam, a concrete block, a shipping container — and attach the loop to the crane's hook. The crane then lifts the whole thing by pulling on the sling.

"The crew wrapped a steel sling around the large boulder before the excavator lifted it out of the trench."

6. A Type of Cocktail (Drink)

A sling is also a classic style of alcoholic drink, usually made with a spirit (most commonly gin), mixed with lemon or lime juice, sugar, and sometimes liqueurs or fruit juices, then served cold in a tall glass. The most famous one in the world is the Singapore Sling, invented at Raffles Hotel in Singapore in the early 1900s.

"He ordered a Singapore Sling and settled into his chair at the bar."

Here is what ties every single meaning above into one idea:

A sling is always a flexible, non-rigid material that does its job by surrounding, supporting, or releasing something. It is never a stiff box or a solid container. It bends around what it holds.

MeaningWhat it cradles or launches
  • The medical sling cradles your arm.
  • The baby sling cradles your child.
  • The weapon sling cradles a stone and then releases it.
  • The carrying sling cradles your rifle or bag on your shoulder.
  • The industrial sling cradles a heavy load for a crane.
  • The cocktail sling "cradles" your drink — a mix held together in a glass.
Which Meanings Do You Encounter Most?

In modern daily life, you'll hear "sling" most often in these situations:

  1. Medical context — "arm in a sling" after an injury. This is by far the most frequent usage today.
  2. Parenting context — "baby sling" or "sling carrier."
  3. Historical/literary context — the weapon sling (especially in stories, scripture, or history).
  4. Travel/bar context — the Singapore Sling cocktail.

The industrial and rifle-sling meanings are more specialized and appear mainly in professional or technical contexts.
One Last Image to Lock It In

Imagine a hammock. It has no rigid frame. It is just fabric that sags, wraps, and holds — perfectly shaped around whatever rests inside it. That is the spirit of a sling. Whether it's holding a broken arm, a baby, a stone about to be launched, a rifle, or a heavy beam — a sling is always that flexible, cradling, wrapping force.
